My family has worked this land in Quzhou for generations. I know what grows here. The soil is deep alluvial loam, the summers are hot and rainy, the winters are dry and cold. There is no question what I will plant — everyone here grows winter wheat then summer maize on the same land. That is what my father did. That is what my neighbors do. That is what works.

I have 8 mu of flat land. I will plant all of it to wheat starting in late September or early October, then turn it straight to maize after the June wheat harvest. Same land, two crops per year. This is how we feed the family and have something to sell.

For wheat seed, I will go to the village seed shop and buy whatever improved variety they recommend — probably Jimai 22 or similar. I won't use old saved seed; that gives lower yield. For maize, I always buy hybrid seed, Xianyu 335 or Zhengdan 958. The shop carries both and they perform well here.

I put down base fertilizer before wheat sowing — diammonium phosphate mixed with urea, tilled in. Then I top-dress urea at jointing stage in spring. I know the ag station says to use less fertilizer but my neighbors who use more get fatter ears, so I use a good amount. I water the wheat three times: once before the ground freezes in November, once at jointing in April, once at heading in May. I spray once for aphids and powdery mildew in spring — one pass usually handles both.

After wheat harvest I plant maize straight into the stubble with the seeder, no need to plough again in summer. Summer rains mostly cover maize water needs; I only irrigate once at planting if the soil is too dry. I spray herbicide right after emergence and check for corn borer in late July — spray if I see it. Harvest maize in late September or early October, then rotary-till for wheat again.
